candidates.source_attribution: Jubilees 40:5 (Joseph rises (40:5)), trans. R.H. Charles, The Book of Jubilees (Oxford: Clarendon, 1902). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And the king commanded that they should arouse Joseph out of the prison: and they arose him out of the prison, and shaved him, and clothed him with new raiment, and presented him before the king' — Jubilees preserves the Gen 41:14 raising-from-prison narrative. Tewahedo Holy-Week Friday-into-Saturday-into-Sunday liturgical pattern reads this as the canonical sequence: Joseph is raised from the pit-prison (cf. tomb), shaved (cf. body-preparation), clothed with new raiment (cf. resurrection-glorification), presented before the king (cf. ascension). The four-fold raised-shaved-clothed-presented sequence is preserved typologically in Tewahedo Easter-day liturgy: the priest enacts each stage in the Resurrection commemoration.

Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And the king said unto Joseph: I have dreamed two dreams, and there is no man who can interpret them. And now I have heard concerning thee, that when thou hearest dreams thou dost interpret them' — Pharaoh acknowledges Joseph's wisdom-from-the-Lord. Jubilees presents Joseph as the canonical-OT example of Spirit-wisdom-given-to-the-rejected-righteous: the prison-vindicated dreamer becomes the interpreter for the king who cannot understand his own dreams. The Tewahedo monastic discernment-tradition (märǝḥǝbǝr — 'spiritual fatherhood' charism) draws on this canonical OT pattern: the genuinely-Spirit-led-interpreter sees what the worldly-king cannot, and the worldly-king must acknowledge his dependence on Spirit-given counsel.

'And he gave him to wife Asenath, the daughter of Potiphar, the priest of Heliopolis, the chief cook' — Jubilees preserves Joseph's marriage to Asenath, the daughter of Potiphar the priest of Heliopolis (later Egyptian apocryphal-Jewish literature substantially develops Asenath's conversion). The Tewahedo tradition of canonical-conversion of Gentile-spouse: Joseph's wife is a Gentile-pagan-priest's daughter, yet she becomes the mother of Ephraim and Manasseh (Israel's continuation). The Tewahedo's distinctive pastoral practice of welcoming and catechizing the Gentile-or-non-Orthodox spouse of an Orthodox member into full sacramental fellowship has its OT canonical anchor in Asenath's reception.
